title: The Practice of Master Hōnen's Teaching
author: The Eighteenth Vow
excerpt: Excerpted from “Editor's Notes,” Chan Magazine, Issue 4, 2000

inline.s: Excerpted from Chan Magazine, 2000
Issue 4, “
Editor's Notes

[Editor's Note]Master Hōnen and his followers have loudly proclaimed: that to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss one “need not cease evil and practice good,” “need not uphold the precepts,” “may commit evil and break the law with impunity,” “the wicked are the true objects of Amitābha Buddha's deliverance,” “recitation of the Name guarantees rebirth,” “the gate of the great vow,” and so on;
see, for details,
The Primal Vow Teaching Is a Pseudo-Buddhist Heresy
Their heretical views
, although they can skillfully exploit human weaknesses to gain a following and speak with dazzling eloquence, are nonetheless false, and what is false is ultimately false
and practice proves everything

What this article exposes about the deeds of the Primal Vow teaching is the concrete practice of those heretical doctrines — “need not cease evil and practice good,” “need not uphold the precepts,” “committing evil and crime is of no consequence,” “the wicked are the true objects of Amitābha Buddha's deliverance,” “recitation of the Name guarantees rebirth,” “the gate of the great vow” —
namely, “the worm within the lion's body that devours the lion's flesh”

. This is the inevitable result of propagating Master Hōnen's system of teaching, which is both lazy and greedy and instigates the breaking of precepts and the doing of evil. Those who are deluded by this not only cannot be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; if one examines their karmic deeds, the retribution awaiting them in the next life can well be imagined. Seeking to ascend, they instead fall — why bring such misery upon oneself!

[The worm in the lion's body] A metaphor for the corrupt members of the monastic community who destroy the Dharma from within. “The worm within the lion's body devours the lion's flesh.” This means that monastics who use the Dharma as a tool to gain fame and profit are not true monastics; they come to destroy the Dharma, to ruin the Dharma, and this is the demon's sole means of extinguishing the Dharma. When Śākyamuni Buddha was alive, the demon king said he would extinguish the Dharma, and the Buddha said: “What I teach is the true Dharma; no one can extinguish it.” The demon king replied: “In the age of the decline of the Dharma, I will have my children all become monastics, don the kasaya robe, and extinguish your Dharma.” Hearing this, the Buddha shed tears, for there was no remedy.

[Both lazy and greedy] Lazy means unwilling to practice diligently, even dreading diligent practice, hoping to reap without sowing; greedy means craving fame, craving profit, craving sensual pleasures, and craving the fruits of attainment. [Seeking to ascend but instead falling]

Teaching the Dharma in a way that contravenes the scriptural meaning, distorts the scriptures, slanders the Buddha, and ruins the Dharma is “impure teaching.” Those who give impure teaching incur extremely grave karmic offenses (greater than seizing the lives of all beings in the three-thousand-great-thousand world system), suffer terribly in retribution (falling into the great hells), and their followers likewise meet a tragic end (entering heresy from which it is hard to return, undergoing all manner of decline and affliction for hundreds of thousands of myriads of lives, with suffering unceasing). The Buddha said
Śāriputra, setting aside the beings of this Jambudvīpa,
if a person were to seize the lives of all beings in the three-thousand-great-thousand world system, the offense of impure teaching is greater than this
. Why is this? Because such a person destroys the anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, aiding the work of the demon,
and likewise causes beings to undergo all manner of decline and affliction for hundreds of thousands of myriads of lives
, able only to bind and not to free. You should know that such a person is an evil teacher to all beings, and with false speech slanders and ruins the Buddhas in the midst of the great assembly,
and for this cause and condition falls into the great hells
Therefore you should know,
that person would rather cut off his own tongue with a sharp knife than give impure teaching in the assembly
(The Buddha Treasury Sutra)

In recent years, many devotees have mailed to this editorial office promotional materials about the Primal Vow teaching of the Japanese True Pure Land school, hoping that Chan Magazine could help propagate them. In their letters they praise and extol the Primal Vow teaching to an extreme degree. They believe that Chinese Buddhism should learn from Japan, and especially that it should learn the Primal Vow teaching, which they regard as the sole hope for the revitalization of Chinese Buddhism. Every time I read such letters, I feel as if an arrow has pierced my heart.

I truly wish that all who study Buddhism would read Elder Dongchu's A Modern History of Chinese Buddhism. Reading that book, you will come to know what is meant by blood and tears, what is meant by great compassion, and what is meant by truly loving one's country and one's religion. I believe that everyone who reads this book will surely be moved to tears by the accounts of the thousands upon thousands of monastics who, risking life and limb, participated in and supported the anti-Japanese national salvation movement and its work of saving the world. I even hope that one day someone will make a vow to bring this history — which moved heaven and earth and made spirits weep — to the screen, for that would surely enable more people to truly feel the boundless compassionate vow of the Buddhist sangha: “Until hell is empty, I vow not to become a Buddha.”

I do not know whether those infatuated with the Primal Vow teaching of the Japanese True Pure Land school are aware that, in modern Chinese history, the monks of the Japanese True Pure Land's Hongan (Primal Vow) branch played an extremely dishonorable role in Japan's invasion of China. As early as the Guangxu reign, the Japanese True Pure Land school established Hongan-ji temples in Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou, Nanjing, and elsewhere, carrying out cultural aggression. Later, seizing the opportunity of the movement to turn temple properties into schools, and under the pretext of protecting Chinese Buddhism, they enticed more than thirty temples in Hangzhou into the embrace of the Japanese True Pure Land school,
and further sought to establish Buddhist academies in order to control the ecclesiastical authority of Chinese Buddhism

(Note: today, with the support of foreign capital, the Primal Vow teaching is vainly attempting to revive its old dream of controlling the ecclesiastical authority of Chinese Buddhism). Fortunately, this scheme was seen through by a group of eminent monks of the time and did not succeed. In those years, the lay devotee Yang Renshan had already criticized the Primal Vow teaching. In 1937, Japan launched its criminal war of all-out aggression against China, and many monks of the Hongan branch of the Japanese True Pure Land school accompanied the army as hired thugs, plundering our Buddhist cultural relics and glorifying the war of aggression. They called the invasion of China a “holy war” to protect Buddhism, declaring that “so long as one believes in Amitābha's Primal Vow, even one who has killed Chinese people can still be reborn,” thereby inciting the Japanese troops' murderous nature.

Just listen to how these Japanese monks who accompanied the army defended their war of aggression: “The Chinese government is a communist government, a Christian government, that destroys Buddhism. Japan is the leader of the Buddhist nations, and in order to protect Buddhism in East Asia we fight against China. This war is a war between Buddhism and Christianity — it is a holy war.”

Now listen to the exposure, made in Burma by the Chinese Buddhist International Walking Propaganda Team led by Master Beiguan, of the ugly faces of the Japanese monks who accompanied the army: “...Since the outbreak of the war of resistance, Japanese monks have embedded themselves among the troops (with at least three to five Japanese monks in every company), instigating the enemy soldiers to slaughter our Buddhist monastics, to violate our Buddhist nuns, and to bomb our Buddhist temples with aircraft and artillery. Judging from all these atrocities, Japan's claim to be a Buddhist nation is entirely hypocritical; it exploits the good name of Buddhism to carry out aggression, using the pretense of Buddhism to conceal its murderous aims...” (Appendix: “On December 1, 1937, before the Japanese army had broken through the gates of Jiangyin, who was it that 'bravely' climbed the city wall along the roofs of the houses and raised the Japanese sun flag, earning the battle honor of being 'first to scale the wall'? It was a military chaplain of Nishi Hongan-ji (the base of Japan's Primal Vow teaching).... On December 12, 1937, the one recognized by the Japanese military as having been the first to charge through a hail of bullets into China's capital — Nanjing — was not a ferocious Japanese soldier priding himself on the samurai spirit, but a military chaplain of Nishi Hongan-ji!” (See the article “Witnessing the History of Aggression”))

We reject the Primal Vow teaching not only because its monastics played an extremely dishonorable role in the process of Japanese militarist aggression against China, but also because it interprets the Pure Land Dharma gate one-sidedly, and even distorts the true spirit of the Dharma!
The Primal Vow teaching dismembers the Pure Land scriptures and teachings,
proclaiming that so long as one believes in the power of Amitābha's Primal Vow, one immediately obtains the passport to rebirth,
with no need to uphold the precepts, no need to practice good, no need to arouse bodhicitta, no need to walk the bodhisattva path, no need to repent,
and that even if one has killed people and set fires, at the moment of death one is assured of rebirth.

The Primal Vow teaching advocates a pure “other-power” doctrine, negating self-power (holding that so long as one believes in the Primal Vow teaching, the Buddha will naturally liberate one without any effort on one's own part, without the need for giving, upholding precepts, or even filial devotion to one's parents). It proclaims “others act, I receive” (the matter of rebirth has already been accomplished for me by the Buddha; I need only believe). It opposes the law of karmic cause and effect (all the evil one has done will be borne by the Buddha for me), and opposes “one reaps what one sows” (no matter what evil one commits, so long as one believes in Amitābha's Primal Vow, the Buddha will surely bear it for one, without the slightest effect on one's rebirth). In this way, the Primal Vow teaching has become the most convenient and easiest liberation teaching in the world.

In Japan, the monastics of the Hongan branch — because one need only believe in Amitābha's Primal Vow and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, with no need to shave the head, no need to uphold the precepts, no need to practice the six perfections, no need to arouse bodhicitta, and one may marry, have children, eat meat, and drink wine — are all
professional monks
, who stay in the temples by day, drawing lots and telling fortunes for people and delivering the dead, and go home at night to enjoy family life.

This runs completely counter to the fine traditions of Chinese Buddhism — shaving the head, wearing monastic robes, eating vegetarian food, remaining celibate, and upholding the precepts. Whether in form or in content, the Primal Vow teaching is a degeneration of Buddhism. Even in Japan, the Hongan branch has been criticized by many other Buddhist schools.

[Shaving the head] Shaving off the hair and beard is the mark of a disciple of the Buddha who has left home; it also signifies the removal of arrogance and distinguishes Buddhist renunciants from the renunciants of other paths. It is the rite of the Buddhas of the three times.

I truly cannot understand how such a deformed religious product has found quite a few people in our country eagerly spreading it, with even some monastics taking part. They distribute materials about the Primal Vow teaching everywhere, call for reforming the traditions of Chinese Buddhism, clamor for learning from Japanese Buddhism and from the Primal Vow teaching, and claim that such a supreme Dharma — so good, so effortless, and so easy to accomplish — was somehow never discovered by the patriarchs of China through the ages!
Undoubtedly, those who are eager to spread the Primal Vow teaching, those who are eager to advocate learning from Japanese Buddhism,
their true aim
is nothing other than to cast off the fine traditions of Chinese Buddhism (traditions which are, to those
false practitioners
, a kind of fetter),

so that, like the monks of Japan's Hongan branch, they can openly enjoy the pleasures of the five desires in this world while still obtaining liberation after death; so that they can accept the offerings and obeisance of devotees as a matter of course and live a comfortable life, without having to work or worry about their livelihood. As for “reforming” or “revitalizing” Buddhism, that is nothing more than their pretense

. This is the mentality of a lazybones who loves ease and hates labor. In terms of mentality, these people are precisely the ones the Buddha spoke of, the ones we in the age of the decline must truly guard against — the
worm within the lion's body
[The worm within the lion's body] “The worm within the lion's body devours the lion's own flesh” is a metaphor for a renunciant monk who destroys the Dharma from within.

It is gratifying that a number of Buddhist periodicals in China have now recognized the harm of the Primal Vow teaching and have published articles exposing and criticizing it. For example, Guangdong Buddhism
, No.
carries Master Long'ang's Do Not Advocate Japan's Primal Vow Teaching; Taizhou Buddhism
, No.

carries Master Fazang's The Unification of Name-Recitation and Reality-Mark Recitation — The Proposal of Primal-Vow Mind Name-Recitation, and Sichuan Lezhi Baoguo Temple's Master Jingkong's Teachings on the Question of Primal-Vow Recitation from His Lectures on the Ksitigarbha Sutra; Pure Land
Summer
carries Master Changzhen's The Three Incompatibilities Between the Primal Vow Teaching and the Pure Land Dharma Gate. These and others are all excellent articles, well worth reading.
To safeguard the purity of Buddhism, our Buddhist community must unambiguously oppose the Primal Vow teaching and stop its spread within the country.
